utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody, and to you, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic, the absence of Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Krgovic, and that's it. Prosecution is a full team today, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Vanderpuye. The witness is present in the courtroom. My idea was to go through some preliminaries, but I think we can postpone that until after she finishes her testimony, if my colleagues are in agreement. So good afternoon, to you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I hadn't the opportunity to welcome you when you started your testimony, so I welcome you today. I understand we have reached the redirect -- the redirect stage so I suggest that we proceed immediately with that, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers should not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will again repeat what the interpreters have just said, please pause since we speak the same language. Pause between questions and answers so that the transcript will truly reflect what we said. After I reviewed the transcript of yesterday, I have but a few additional questions for you today. Yesterday, my colleague Mr. Prosecutor at page 27540, lines 9 to 11, read out a part of Mr. Gavric's statement concerning some other patients. I will quote this in English. [In English] "The nurse mentioned that she did not feel good about the assignment since her brother had been killed during the war." [Interpretation] Do you remember this part of the text?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At your pediatrics ward during the war, did any of the nurses mention that she felt uncomfortable treating Muslim children?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jovicic, yesterday you were asked a number of questions concerning the events at the pediatrics ward in June 1995 concerning a boy who was admitted into the Zvornik hospital. I will put a straightforward question. For my colleagues, the reference is page 7593, lines 19 to 23, of the transcript in this case. My question is this, after you took over your duty, as you said yesterday, on the 16th of July, 1995, did you hear that a nurse at the pediatrics ward picked up a chair, trying to hit Dr. Gotovac because in July 1995 she admitted a Muslim boy to the ward?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is this an incident that you would be informed about as one of the duty physicians had it happened?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Does this fall within the domain of professional and interrelationship communication when taking over shifts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer that question. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, these questions were actually asked and answered. They were posed on the direct examination of the witness. I don't see a basis for leading this witness on redirect examination of the exact same questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will understand I will have to refer to my colleagues on that because when she started her evidence yesterday I wasn't here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being told by my colleagues that Mr. Vanderpuye is essentially correct. However, since I haven't asked you to comment on his objection, perhaps you may have some other reason why you have repeated the question which has already been answered, if you could explain that, Ms. Nikolic. Unless you prefer to move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put this question for the sole reason that my colleague during cross-examination raised the issue of incidents and the way such incidents are treated and dealt with at various levels in the Zvornik hospital. That is why I wanted to clarify this point from the transcript. Of course, the question is not identical to the one I put during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Doctor, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jovicic, would you like me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even realise there was a question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would this be an event that would fall within the domain of professional and interpersonal communication when physicians take over shifts between each other?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is that something that would be talked about in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, since this would be from the professional domain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have one last question, or rather, I would like to hear your opinion. During the entire war and post-war period, what was the relationship with all of the physicians at the pediatrics wards with the children of Muslim -- with the Muslim children who were treated?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I dealt with that in detail yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object. It calls for a narrative and it's completely irrelevant in respect of the specific issues that the witness was addressed -- that I addressed with the witness on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Nikolic, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend during cross-examination raised the issue of an incident which had to do with Dr. Gavric's statement. I would like the witness to explain what was the treatment of Muslim patients like at their ward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We acted humanely and in accordance with all international regulations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to say -- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam, you would have for sure understood that there was a question or a dispute between the Prosecution and the Defence whether you should answer this question at all. So please wait until we decide whether it's a legitimate question or not before you proceed any further. If necessary I will strike it off from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on. But if this happens again, Doctor, please wait until we decide whether you should give the answer or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone to her right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no further questions for you, madam, which means that you are free to go. You will receive assistance from our staff. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone, I wish you is a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, exhibits. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our list was handed over. I believe it includes only the statement of this witness that is being tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Mr. President. I would only ask that the documents, the statements, rather, be tendered under seal because they contain sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Any objections from anyone else? No. So the document will be admitted under seal as suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have any documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I have no documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That concludes the testimony of the witness. Now, let me revert to what I had planned for the beginning of the sitting. There is a recent, as recent as yesterday actually, motion from the Borovcanin Defence team called the Borovcanin Defence second motion for admission of written evidence in lieu of oral testimony pursuant to Rule 92 bis which is accompanied by an appendix, quite a bulky one. As a starter, does the Prosecution take a position on this motion or do you require more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not one I've looked at and I have been talking to Mr. Lazarevic about some things and I don't recall if that's one of them or not, so I think we would need a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There is, however, another motion in which Borovcanin requested the admission of a statement by a certain brigadier general, I won't mention his name in case he might wish to be protected, again pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Without cross-examination, of course, for 92 bis. And have you looked at this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is the one that I spoke to Mr. Lazarevic about and I think we were very close to reaching some kind of an agreement on it but I'll continue that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, then there is -- during my absence there was the issue of the Nikolic motion for the testimony of two individuals, Witnesses 3DW8 and 3DW9 to be heard via conference link. This was filed confidentially on the 8th of September. We have discussed this and we have -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Just to let the Trial Chamber know that, of course, we have been drafting a reply which will be filed tonight because we filed this motion, the Prosecution objected in its response, and we are within the normal time frame to file our reply today, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we are dispensing you from -- exempting you from the need to file this reply. We have considered the reasons put forward by the Nikolic Defence team for the testimony of these individuals to be heard via conference link and we have also considered the objection or the opposition of the Prosecution. When we have weighed the two positions, we have come to the conclusions that -- the conclusion that the reasons brought by the Prosecution in opposition to the motions are not sufficiently weighty to justify the denial of the motion, which seems to us to be justified. And therefore, we are granting the motion and the preparations need to be put in place immediately by liaising Mr. Bourgon and Ms. Nikolic, with the relative staff members to have this organised. We haven't got a clue as to when they are expected to give evidence, that does not transpire as such with clarity, so you need to do this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We were -- we have already been in contact with the staff from the registry in the event the motion was granted to set a date and this would be likely on the 24th of September and we will continue our liaison work with the registry staff. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, there is the other matter which was raised about three weeks ago by Madam Fauveau which received practically an across the floor, across-the-floor support from the other Defence teams as well as the Prosecution. You have asked for a break in these proceedings to enable you to cope with perusing the voluminous amount of new material that has been given to you by the Prosecution. We have considered primarily the nature of your request. We do not, of course, for a moment think that it is a capricious request. We also have considered the amount of material that needs to be perused in respect of whether ultimately it shows up to be important or not for these cases. Actually from what I could gather at the time that submissions were made, not even the Prosecution had the time to go through these documents and see for themselves whether they were relatively important for these proceedings. We do not, however, feel that all the time that you have requested can be justified, especially since the various Defence cases here are staggered. If anything, for example, the position of the Nikolic Defence team is -- would call for more understanding. Same applies to the Borovcanin Defence team. We believe that if we grant you the limited break that we are going to mention, it should be enough. Then obviously as we have done in the past, should later on after you have concluded this exercise, should it transpire that there is fresh information, new information that justifies us going back and provide a remedy, then of course we will do so. However, we have considered a little bit where we stand, also how we are proceeding and we have decided to grant a break in these proceedings starting from the 13th of October until the 17th. Basically, although on the face of it that looks like five days, it is more than that. You have actually from the 11th until the 19th. We have also chosen that week because the following week is a shorter week. Instead of a five day week, it's a four day week, 24th October being a UN holiday. So you will have further three days at the end of the subsequent week which should according to us help you cope with the difficult situation that has arisen. Okay. So that was all that I wanted to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are two issues I would like to bring to the Court's attention at this time. The first one in relation to the scheduling instruction we have just received. It is just to inform the Trial Chamber that it is our intention to try and end the presentation of the case for the Defence of Drago Nikolic by Friday, the 3rd of October. Of course we don't know whether that will be possible or not. We will do our best to finish the presentation of our case within a time period of three weeks. That being said, I've already had some discussions with my colleague from the Prosecution concerning a specific day that they want to change a witness, and we are continuing to talk about this specific date. That was the first issue, Mr. President. The second issue is something that was brought to my attention just before the beginning of this court session today and I need to go into private session, Mr. President, to speak about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. So next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Sakotic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome. You are about to start --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been summoned here as a witness by the Defence team for Drago Nikolic. Before you start your testimony, which hopefully as expected will be a short one, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath in certain jurisdictions, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of this declaration, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sakotic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a 92 ter witness, so you know what the procedure is, Ms. Nikolic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sakotic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We've already met?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But I will state my fame for the record. My name is Jelena Nikolic and I represent Mr. Nikolic. Would you be so kind as to tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: My name is Mirko Sakotic. I live in Zvornik. I work in the Birac factory. I was born on the 5th of March, 1952, in Donji Davidovici in Bilice municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where do you live today, and where do you work?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, the counsel is kindly asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I currently live in Zvornik and I work in the Birac factory in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What education do you have, what kind of degree do you hold, how are you qualified for your job?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I am a technician which means that I completed two years of vocational college.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, do you recall having given a statement to Drago Nikolic's Defence on the 5th of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave this statement. It was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read your statement before signing it and in the few days before your appearance here in Court in the course of your proofing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an opportunity to read it then and I also read it now just before my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because we are proceeding under Rule 92 ter, I will now read a summary of your statement for the record. The witness lives in Zvornik and is employed as a technician in the Birac factory in Zvornik. The witness was mobilised on the 1st of June, 1992, and remained mobilised until the 17th of January, 1992. Then he was mobilised again on the 12th of August, 1994, and this lasted until the 29th of October, 1994, in the Zvornik Brigade in the traffic and transport section which was in the rear. The assistant commander for logistics of the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995 was Sreten Milosevic. The witness stated that the role of the transport and traffic department or section was to receive oral orders, to dispatch vehicles. This was done on the orders of the commander through the assistant commander for logistics. The witness's immediate superior was Radislav Pantic, the chief for transport and traffic in the Zvornik Brigade. The witness remembers that the vehicle would be dispatched on a mission depending on the number of personnel and the quantity of ammunition, food, and other stuff that needed to be transported and the type of terrain where the vehicle was to be sent. The transport and traffic department would dispatch a vehicle and the driver who was in charge of that vehicle and each vehicle had a driver assigned to it. Sometimes in the vehicle log the names of other drivers, replacement drivers, would also be entered. All the tasks for the transport and traffic department were set during the morning operational briefings of the brigade and were relayed to the department, the transport and traffic department, through the assistant commander for logistics, or in his absence, the commander of the logistics battalion or, in other cases, duty operational officers could issue tasks to the transport and traffic department. The witness recalls that in July 1995 Radislav Pantic was absent because of a death in his family. In Pantic's absence, either the witness himself or Miso Pavicevic would sign the travel orders or vehicle logs. The witness explained how this document was filled in and what it contained. The witness knows Djordje Gotovac who was a driver in the Zvornik Brigade and he drove a van. The witness explained the travel order, ERN 0069465300694654, for a Volkswagen van D2, with Djordje Gotovac designated as the driver, and he remembers that the column with the actual routes for the 14th of July, 1995, does not correspond to the capabilities of the vehicle, the mileage, and that the mileage actually does not tally with the number of trips. The witness recognizes his signature on the order for the D2 Volkswagen van and remembers that he was on duty in the transport and traffic department of the brigade on the 14th of July, 1995. According to the travel order and to the best of his recollection, Djordje Gotovac was dispatched to Uzice in Serbia on that day. The witness remembers that Djordje Gotovac did not receive an order to take his vehicle to Orahovac on that day. To the best of his recollection, the witness believes that Djordje Gotovac never asked for days off from the witness during the war, nor was the witness authorised to approve any request for days off, or any leave for the drivers. Just a moment, let me check something. Something has been left unclear in the transcript, but I will clarify this in my examination. The witness speaks about the special procedure about the filling in of travel orders for the battalion. Each battalion had its assistants for logistics and this person was in charge of assigning the vehicles and using the vehicles. The battalion assistant for logistics signed the travel orders. The witness explains that travel order ERN number 0069489800694899 for a D2 Mercedes vehicle with Veljko Ivanovic and Vukasin Peric designated as its drivers, claiming that there is no signature of his on that document. The witness assumes that the signature on the order is that of the battalion assistant commander for logistics in the second battalion. The witness confirms that the use of the vehicle listed on this travel order was within the jurisdiction of the battalion commander, Sreco Acimovic. Explaining the procedure for the use of vehicles in the battalions, the witness confirms that the battalion commander would issue orders to the driver on the use of the vehicle because both the vehicles and the drivers were fully within the jurisdiction of the battalion. The transport and traffic department of the brigade had one obligation only, and that was to issue fuel to the battalion on a monthly basis to cover its needs, and then this quantity would be delivered to the battalions in barrels, and then they used it as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This completes my summary of your statement under Rule 92 ter. Mr. Sakotic, now, I would like to ask you whether this summary that I've just read reflects what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The facts contained in your statement, are they true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do they reflect accurately what you would have said to the Judges had you been asked to describe those events?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment I would like to tender into evidence document 3D473, that is Mr. Mirko Sakotic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would take it there's no objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Other Defence teams? None. Okay, yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like to ask some questions in order to get a more detailed explanation of some of the things that he put in his statement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, could you please explain to us the structure of the transport and traffic department in the Zvornik Brigade and how many personnel were there in that department?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The transport and traffic department of the Zvornik Brigade functioned in the following manner. There was a platoon of drivers, part of the logistics battalion, there was a chief and two desk officers who were in the brigade command. They were a separate service. They provided the logistics for the transportation of the personnel, equipment, material, everything that had to do with transportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The three desk officers that you told us about, what was the nature of their job?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the chief and two desk officers. We received our assignments from the assistant commander for logistics regarding the activities that were planned for each day, and in accordance with the requests, we would dispatch vehicles, we would provide the vehicles with enough fuel to complete the mission and we would just dispatch them on their way. We had those regular routes, every day rotation of personnel in the brigade, transportation of food, so those were our daily tasks. We knew those were standing orders. We didn't have to receive specific orders to that effect every day. We knew what to do and nothing changed in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, who was the chief of the transport department in the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995, and who were the desk officers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The chief of the department was Antic [as interpreted], Radislav. He had a degree in transportation engineering. The desk officers were myself Mirko Sakotic and Miso Pavicevic I think he joined the brigade in 1995, or rather, that's when he joined this department of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You've told us that the drivers were part of the logistics battalion. Who was the commander of the logistics battalion in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: It was Radivoje Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the chief of the transport and traffic department because it was not recorded accurately in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Radislav Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your proofing, you were able to note an error in your statement and now I would like us to clarify that. In July 1995, in the transport and traffic department, who did you receive orders from and how?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: All the orders -- and this goes not only for July but throughout this period, all the orders came from the assistant commander for logistics through the battalion -- logistics battalion commander and, in their absence, the orders could be issued by the duty officer. The duty operations officer as we called him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, did you ever receive any orders from other assistant commanders or chiefs of staff such as the chief of engineers, chief of security?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No, this was not the usual practice and if -- they probably talked to the assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was dispatching engineering vehicles part of your jurisdiction, of the purview of the transport and traffic department?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No, the engineers had their own fleet of vehicles. They carried out their tasks using their own vehicles. Our role in all this was to issue fuel in accordance with the orders that also specified the quantity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did you receive your orders, orally or in writing, from the assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did those oral orders contain a description of the nature of the task why a vehicle was to be dispatched to a certain location?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us why the desk officers, why the transport and traffic department did not receive information about the nature of the task that the vehicles would be used for?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: In the military, some information is confidential and if such information were to be disseminated to reach each and every soldier, then you would have no discipline, no nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us something about a travel order that is part of your statement, 92 ter statement. Could we please have page 109 of P295. Mr. Sakotic, you will see in front of you on the screen a document. That's P295. Have you seen this document as you were preparing for giving your statement and for your testimony here today, Mr. Sakotic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: This is a form for a travel order or a vehicle log. Each vehicle had this and as you can see it was typed in, and this was done in our department. Information about the vehicle, consumption, what kind of fuel, and the name of the driver. If the driver's name changed, then a new name would be added, but as a rule, each vehicle had a designated driver and there was also the signature of the chief of the transport and traffic department down there in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When would you fill in those items?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: At the end of any given month we would do that for the following month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record -- blinking -- now it's connected. Thank you. Just to clarify for the record, the witness just indicated that he recognised a signature somewhere in the corner. If we could just specify that for the record which signature it is since there are a number of signatures on this page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will agree to that, I am sure, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page -- Mr. Prosecutor, on the front page, that's item 2, in the lower right-hand corner you have the signatures of Pantic, Radislav, the chief of the department. It says here transport and traffic desk officer, Radislav Pantic would sign that, and in his absence, I would do that or the other desk officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was this part of the travel order filled in and when was it signed, this part that you said was typed in in your department and then it was signed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: It was done at the end of a month for the following month.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The other pages of the travel order, were they filled in at the same time when this information was filled in and when the front page was signed by the transport and traffic desk officer?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: All the rest was blank.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we look at this document, you can see the middle column where you have some entries written by hand, information about the receipt of fuel and lubricant. So who would fill in this middle part of the document, who made those entries?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The middle part of the document was filled in by whoever issued the order for the fuel to be issued, and here where you see it says signature of handlers, those were soldiers who were filling the vehicles up at the gas station.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the front page here, do you know -- can you recognise anyone's handwriting, any of the handlers and the names of the drivers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: You can see the names of the drivers are Djordje Gotovac, Bosko Babic and Djuric Milic. And I recognise the signature of Mile or Milenko Nikolic, one of the handlers. I don't know his exact name but his nickname was Mile. And Stevo Gajic too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we now move on to the next page of this document. That's page 110 in e-court. Mr. Sakotic, can you see this fairly well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you who fills in the second page of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The second page of this document, date, time, whoever needs the vehicle, the route, the mileage, number of trips, and so on, that's filled in by the driver. And column number 20 is filled in by the desk officer or the chief, whoever signed the travel order fills in this part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In this travel order, do you know which of the drivers filled it in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously this is Djoko Gotovac. This is all his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if Mr. Pantic was present at his workplace in the traffic and transport department in the brigade on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No, he was not there. He had a death in his family, his mother died, so he was not there. He was not in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, have a look at this work log and try to locate the 14th of July entries.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Concerning the entry for the 14th of July, who was the desk officer who signed off as the user?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: As you can see, it was myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Please explain this vehicle movement on the 14th of July. What sort of an order did the driver, Mr. Gotovac, receive?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Looking at the order, I can tell you that Gotovac on that day went to Uzice. As for the route, Zvornik-Uzice, that means he set out at 6 o'clock, it's something that seems to be changed, I don't know whether it was 5 or 6 that day. As for the relation, the distance and the route, it says Zvornik-Uzice loko.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When did you sign this travel order for Mr. Gotovac, what time of day would you usually do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The driver must not set off without a neatly filled in travel order. In particular the route needs to be noted and signed by the person who ordered the trip to be made. That is the traffic desk officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that you signed this before the driver left, in this case it was Djordje Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a possible that I signed it either on July, late in the evening, or the 14th, early in the morning, because he left for Uzice early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 3D484 in e-court. While waiting for it, I will ask you this: In the proofing for your testimony, you did some calculations according to the data on the order and you made some of your markings or rather you noted some things down. Could you please explain to the Chamber what your conclusions were when you started this travel order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: We should have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That is page 2 of 3D484. Before I ask you anything, I wanted to ask you this: Mr. Sakotic, the additional numbers, the figures on the order, whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Mine. I made these notes during the proofing. I did that because I was curious about the kilometres. It struck me as unusual, six trips, 50 people on the route between Zvornik and Uzice. It is 130 kilometres one way which would mean 260 kilometres for one trip, and according to the data here, we have 402 kilometres. For six trips, he should have made 1.560 kilometres. It struck me as odd. Obviously the travel order was not filled in properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the entry for the 13th of July, 1995. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The driver on the 13th of July went from Zvornik to Mali Zvornik and then to Celopek. As far as I can recall, the distance is some 79 kilometres. He left at 7 a.m., returned at 2 a.m., that is 19 hours in total that he spent driving that route which one can complete in an hour. I did not issue him with any order of that sort. I was the one issuing the order for the 14th only.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, 1995, did you order Djordje Gotovac to go and perform an additional task to take food and drinks to the soldiers in Orahovac at the school there, and did you do that orally?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. That was in the travel order. Orahovac is a trip on its own. It is not something that would fall under the loko item.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If we look at the loko for the 14th of July 1995, what does this loko refer to, and this issue ordered to Djordje Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: When the driver set off from Zvornik to Uzice he can only, of course, note down Zvornik-Uzice. In Uzice, if there was any local movement, he inserts Loko and then that should have been followed by a dash and then Zvornik to indicate that he returned to the base. Therefore, I see this only as local movement in Uzice itself. Otherwise, when we would dispatch drivers, for precaution we would always supply them with a bit more fuel than they would regularly need to cover that trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You've already answered that on the 14th of July you did not dispatch Gotovac to perform any other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Pantic was absent on the 14th and 15th of July, did Djordje Gotovac ask you for any days off, in particular on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he ever ask you for any leave? As best you can recall, do you remember such an event?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No, for the simple reason that we could not approve any leave for Djordje Gotovac. He wasn't part of our unit. He was a member of the rear battalion, had his own commander and it was his commander who could approve his leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you said "we" could not approve any leave for him, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: The drivers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the transport section?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Any of the soldiers there. It was three of us there and it was all done through the assistant commander for logistics. We could not go on leave without his approval and we in turn could not approve anyone's leave because we did not have our subordinates. We were independent, and we were plain soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could we please have in e-court 3D51 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 3D311.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3DP311. Attendance records of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, you have seen this document during proofing. In item 23 there is a name, it says Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, item 23 Pantic, Radislav. Father's same Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom out so that we would be able to see the dates as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Concerning the 13th, 14th and 15th of July, can you tell us what are the markings concerning Radislav Pantic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: It says on leave, on leave, on leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in a few words, what was the functioning of transport like in the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Each battalion had its own rolling stock that they could use to perform their regular duties. By that, I mean the transport of soldiers for shift rotations. Some battalions were assisted by us because they did not have sufficient number of vehicles. They had an ambulance and a command vehicle as well. They had tractors used to take food to the frontlines which were difficult to access. In short, they had their own fleet of vehicles independent of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who ordered the use of vehicles in the battalions? Who issued orders?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Probably on battalion commander's orders through the assistant commander for logistics, and down to the drivers. That would be the usual hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You mean assistant commander for logistics in battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In some units you even had traffic and transport desk officers, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P295 in e-court next. Page 354, 355 in B/C/S and 355 to 358 in the English. However, let us start with 345 [as interpreted] in the B/C/S and 355 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document -- yes, Mr. Sakotic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, and I'm familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is it? A travel order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. A travel order of the second battalion. The commander was Sreco Acimovic. Logistics assistant commander, I think his name was Pisic, aka Zico. The drivers were Peric, Vukasin, and Ivanovic, Veljko.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When we look at page 1 of this travel order, the part that is typed in and then we see a signature by a desk officer. Please explain to us how come it was Mr. Pantic's signature on this battalion travel order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Battalions, much as brigades, keep their transport archives with the brigade, to the traffic section there, towards the end of any month. This was blank and then the same way we treated it it would be filled in the previous month for the next month. They could not be issued with another new order without having filled in the old one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the situation like with the fuel issued in relation to the battalion travel orders?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: It is signed by everyone who took part, those who issued fuel, those who received it. In the column where it says 118 in total, where we have a further breakdown of how much was meant to be spent, how much was spent in fact, and then we have the signature as well. This had to be filled in before this order would be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about the column user signature, that's the last column, or the operator signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It's the last rectangle, whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Pisic, Zico or Zivojin, assistant commander for logistics in the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did battalions receive fuel in any other way except by fueling their vehicles at the gas station of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Since there were problems with the supply of fuel, it was known which battalion could be issued with how much fuel for their needs. In most cases, they would receive that fuel in cannisters or barrels and then they would use that in their own respective brigades as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at page 2 of the document. In the B/C/S 355, in the English 356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. There's a delay on my microphone coming on, I apologise. Just before we get to the next question, just a clarification at line 29 -- sorry, page 29, line 15, my LiveNote doesn't record the name that the witness provided as the assistant commander for logistics in the second battalion. It's line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic, I think Mr. Thayer is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think it was line 23 because I see the sign that something is missing there. I will clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sakotic, what was the name of the assistant commander for logistics in the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, it was Pisi c. His first name was either Zivan or Zivojin. His nickname was Zico.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Pesic or Pisic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Pisic. P-i-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It seems that it is incorrect again. Please tell us again. Spell it for us.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: P-i-s-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 2 and tell us who filled in the second page on the travel order for the drivers from this battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: As you can see from this order it is quite apparent that this is filled in by the drivers using the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And who affixes the signature in column 20, signature of user?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: That would be the drivers who drove the vehicle on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And at the end of this column 20, the last signature down there, the signature of the person approving it, whose signatures is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: That is Pisic's signature. He calculated the mileage and the fuel consumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the handwriting of any of the drivers on this order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see Peric, P, Vukasin, and Ivanovic, Veljko Ivanovic. I assume that that would be Veljko, the driver. And there is a signature, Vlado -- I don't know really. I think he was a desk officer in the technical service, that would be Vlado Acimovic, so it's possible that it is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, although you may already have given me a partial answer to this question, those drivers, Veljko Ivanovic and others, on whose orders did drivers from the 2nd Battalion go on mission in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: On the orders of the battalion commander, I assume, and the orders of the battalion. It is quite obvious from the way this is filled in that they had nothing to do with the brigade. This was a battalion vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Sreco Acimovic was the commander of the battalion throughout the whole time, which includes that specific time period too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sreco Acimovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Acimovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other cross-examinations? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not cross-examining this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, do you prefer to start now or after the break? We can have the break now, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That would be my preference, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you expect your cross-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I've estimated an hour. I'll try to come in under that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The next witness is ready here, Mr. Bourgon or Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Nelson Thayer, I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, in July of 1995, Captain First Class Sreten Milosevic was the assistant commander for logistics in the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know who preceded him in that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I believe it was Nikolic. I don't recall the first name. Lieutenant -- well, it was Nikolic. But before him it was Miso Kanostrelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the Nikolic to whom you were referring, was his first name possibly Bosko, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Bosko, yes. Bosko Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber when it was that Captain Milosevic took over from Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is Bosko Nikolic any relation to security chief Drago Nikolic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may see 65 ter 3742 briefly, please. And if we could scroll over on the B/C/S just a little bit to the left. Thank you, that's perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing you what is a page from the Zvornik Brigade phone directory, and I just want to turn your attention to about the middle of the page where it indicates the chief of the traffic and transport service and there are four names, all of which you mentioned in your evidence in chief. Radislav Pantic; yourself, Mirko Sakotic; Milorad Pavicevic; and Radivoje Obradovic. I note also -- if you go up a bit you'll see a listing for the assistant commander for logistics, Second Lieutenant Bosko Nikolic. Sir, you testified that your recollection was that Milorad Pavicevic joined the brigade sometime in 1995. I note here that this doesn't list Captain Milosevic as the assistant commander for logistics and I'm just wondering if this helps you help the Court determine approximately what date in 1995 Mr. Milosevic became the assistant commander for logistics? Can you put any period of time in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. And Radivoje Obradovic, I don't know, he never was in the transport and traffic department, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, this indicates that Mr. Pavicevic had been in the brigade for some period of time if he preceded Mr. Milosevic in the rear units; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Milosevic was the assistant commander for logistics and that Milorad Pavicevic came in that period too. I think he was in one of the battalions, the 3rd Battalion. I don't know, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, you've referred to Mr. Pavicevic by the nickname Miso; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pantic's nickname was Panto; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Panto. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you we are done with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it almost goes without saying, sir, that during the war fuel was a precious resource and the army had to keep very close track of it at every level, from the battalion all the way up to the Main Staff; do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to see whether you agree or disagree with some information that Mr. Pantic shared with the authorities in Sarajevo in an interview he gave and also with us, the OTP, in an interview he gave to us in 2007 as well. When he was interviewed by the Prosecutor's Office in Sarajevo, and for my friends this is at paragraph 15 of the SIPA statement. That's page 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. We can put that up as 3736. He said that he and yourself, sir, kept accurate records of the daily consumption of fuel and that the technical administration was in charge of the total consumption of fuel within the brigade. Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when he was interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in 2007 -- and this is page 14. I'm just going to try to save some time and we won't put it up on the e-court. He told us that you were very careful about filling out the transportation logs, the vehicle work orders, and making sure that the paperwork was in order before a vehicle could leave the barracks and that that was a way also to control the use of the vehicles and prevent misuse or unauthorized use of the vehicles. Do you agree with that statement as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He described how a vehicle would not be able to leave the barracks unless yourself or someone else on your behalf or on Pantic's behalf signed off and said that they could leave with one of those vehicle logs. Do you agree with that, sir? That's at page 17 of the OTP statement.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, he was asked a specific question about engineering equipment, engineering vehicles, and with respect to those types of vehicles he said, and this is at page 5 of the statement in Sarajevo, both the English and the B/C/S. He said: "Myself, Mirko Sakotic and Miso Pavicevic would usually sign the first page." I think that's consistent with what you said today; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So let me just ask you, putting aside the specific situation of engineering vehicles, is it also true that in general with respect to regular trucks, vans or other vehicles, any three of you could sign the work orders?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And which way is that not correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I will make just one correction. If, if Pantic or somebody else, because there was a shortage of vehicles, usually those were just those small trucks or something like that. So if there was a possibility for us to do something and we didn't have the vehicles, we could call the engineers, the engineers commander and ask them to give us their vehicle, and then we would sign the travel order. But that happened very rarely. I don't recall having ever signed such an order, and I don't know whether Pantic did or not. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, my question wasn't clear, sir. What I was trying to ask you was, putting aside occasions where engineering equipment was at issue, just in general during your day-to-day work in the traffic services unit, with respect to the day in and day out vehicles logs, be it a TAM 130 or a Volkswagen van or what have you, is it true that any one of the three of you could sign off on those logs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: We could sign the blank travel orders and we would give it to them at the beginning of the month, but they had to hand in the old vehicle logs or travel orders. In other words, no new travel orders could be issued for any vehicles unless the old travel order for the previous month was correctly filled in and then handed in. And I don't know who did that, who took care of that, their assistant commander or somebody like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But just to be clear, when those blank travel orders were filled in at the end of the month for the next month, it could have been yourself, Mr. Pantic or Mr. Pavicevic who could have signed that; is that fair to say? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, what you are saying is correct. And we prepared those logs at the end of the month. So in the period between the 25th and the 30th, whenever we had some spare time, we would prepare them for each unit, those blank forms, but we would just fill in the front page where it said the type of the vehicle, drivers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, we'll look at some specific examples in a little while, but on these forms, usually on the left-hand side, there is a column that asks for a condition of the vehicle or a description of the condition of the vehicle, and that was also something that someone in your position would sign off on before the vehicle was released; is that correct? It had to be listed in working or not working order or some assessment of the condition of the vehicle had to be attested to by a signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the back, the last page of the travel order, this is where you certified the -- that the vehicle was in good working order. Usually this was done by the technical service that did the maintenance. We in the logistics battalion -- well, there are quite a few of the signatures that belong to me, to Pantic, and somebody from the technical service, Milic or whoever. Sometimes it was difficult to find this man, he was out on a task somewhere and the vehicle had to go out, somebody would sign it there. And every time a vehicle would go out on a trip, on the return the -- it was verified whether it was in good working order and then a certification was made to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sometimes, if I understand what you are telling us, sir, if that individual that couldn't be found was not around, that somebody who would sign off on the condition of the vehicle would be yourself or one of the -- or the other desk officer Mr. Pavicevic or Mr. Pantic himself; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, for logistics vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these work orders, these vehicle logs, if I understand your testimony correctly, when a driver receives his task for the day, before he can leave with the vehicle, he has to have a route filled in on that log in order for him to be approved to leave Standard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And once the trip is filled in by the driver, then one of us desk officers signed it and issued fuel for that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's before he even turns the key, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it was the case, was it not, that if a driver were given an additional assignment or even more than one additional assignment during the day, particularly if that assignment was local, it would happen that that local trip might be listed simply eventually as "local" on the log later; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, local trips would be maybe a distance of 2 or 3 kilometres, the surrounding area around the barracks, the gas station in Zvornik. So that was considered as a local trip, local.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it was the case, was it not, sir, that surely there were occasions when a driver who was given a number of such local tasks during a given day, particularly if those additional tasks were issued at the end of the day, might not even record the fact that he went to a local destination in the vehicle log?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, but it's possible that this might have happened, but the mileage was very low here. As a rule, anyone who went anywhere had to record it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, sir. Now, you testified in your evidence in chief that you were not told the nature of the assignment when it was given orally, or that the drivers were not given the nature of their assignment when it was given to them orally. I just want to ask you a couple of questions about that, sir. Doesn't a driver need to know certain basic things about the nature of his tasks? For example, what is it that he is going to be carrying in the back of his truck, whether it's ammunition, whether it's something that's very heavy, whether it's something that is human, wounded people to a hospital, soldiers to a frontline? Don't the drivers need to know certain information about the nature of their task so that they know and you know that the right vehicle, the appropriate vehicle is being dispatched for the task at hand?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, in an oral order it is stated, Send a TAM truck to transport 15 soldiers from here to there, or send a TAM truck to the ammo to transport a certain quantity of ammunition. So we didn't specify anything. We simply knew that. We were told that. We always knew the number of soldiers in each shift. We always had the appropriate vehicles. If you had two or three people, you would always -- you would never send a truck but some other vehicle. If somebody was wounded, you would not send a truck, there were other vehicles and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, one thing you said before we broke that kind of stuck in my mind, sir, was with respect to one of the vehicle logs, particularly the one that involved Mr. Veljko Ivanovic. You suggested that that was strictly a battalion log and that it had nothing to do with the brigade. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware, first of all, sir, that that very record was seized from the Zvornik Brigade pursuant to a search warrant in 1998, not from any battalion but from the brigade itself? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: During the proofing I saw some orders and this is how I learned that, in fact, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it fair to say given what you've told the Trial Chamber about the importance of fuel and the importance of knowing what the various logistics needs are within the brigade, be it for fuel, food, ammunition, that such a record that you spoke about and identified as being simply a battalion document had everything to do with the brigade because it was the brigade that needed to know and what the use demands were within the battalions in order to understand what the brigade had available in its reserves and what it could issue out to the various battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I didn't really understand the thrust of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question is, sir, the document that you spoke about, that you identified as coming from the 2nd Battalion, that has everything to do with the brigade, does it not, sir, because it's precisely these vehicle logs that you were using day in and day out to ensure the fuel usage was appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: But we didn't fill in anything on any of the vehicle logs or travel orders apart from those items that were typed in. Everything else was filled in by the battalion. If they had any emergency demands, they would get their fuel either from the brigade or from some donors. I really don't know. We simply filled in what was on the front page and the desk officer or the chief of the transport and traffic service would affix his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, weren't these work orders, these vehicle logs, an important link between the brigades and the battalions to keep track of the logistics needs of the brigade, and of the battalions in turn?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, all the travel orders were kept in the brigade by us, from battalions too, and battalions could not get new travel orders if they hadn't handed in the old ones that recorded specifically the fuel consumption, the mileage, and it had to be certified by a responsible person, the assistant commander for logistics or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let's move on. Just one last question about Mr. Pantic's conversations with us. Again, with respect to occasions when equipment had to be mobilised, say from Birac Holding, for the brigade's use, Mr. Pantic told us that if the mobilisation of that equipment was large, the request would come from one of three people; Sreten Milosevic, Dragan Obrenovic, or Vinko Pandurevic. Do you agree with Mr. Pantic's statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I really am not the chief of the transport and traffic department, I don't have the information that Pantic had at his disposal, so I really don't know how this mobilisation proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the week or so following the takeover by the VRS of the Srebrenica enclave on 11 July 1995. I think we'll all agree that you were on duty during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And say for the week to ten days following 11 July, were you sleeping in the barracks or sleeping at Standard or were you permitted to go home at night, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Mostly at Standard. Sometimes people went home to take a bath or something. I don't recall whether I was there every night, but most of the nights, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And because vehicles would be returning to Standard at all hours of the night or being needed at any time during the day or night, someone had to remain on duty in your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that person would be awakened if there is a need for anything of the sort. They all knew where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pavicevic was also staying in the barracks as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when Mr. Pantic was absent from the 10th to the 15th of July, you and Mr. Pavicevic were there the entire time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Most likely. Perhaps we would just go to our homes and then quickly come back, but we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you went home, Mr. Pavicevic would cover for you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this period of time, you would agree that you in fact did go home at some point during this ten-day period to shower, as you said, or see your family or perhaps have a hot meal?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: To take a shower and to see my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again I'm speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask my learned friend to be more precise about the period he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're referring to a ten-day period. I would assume that Ms. Nikolic only wants to know the beginning and the end of these ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we've been referring to the ten days, as I said, following the fall of the Srebrenica on the 11th of July. Has that been your understanding during this questioning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you some documents and I'm going to try to move through them as quickly as I can. I want to show you some signatures and ask you some questions about some of the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P00295, and we'll be looking at pages 37 and 38 of both the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You see a document -- an original document in your own language in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as we can see, this is vehicle work log for a Zastava 35.8; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you if you can identify some of these signatures. If we look at the lower right-hand corner at number 2, the signature line. You recognise that signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is Radislav Pantic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look almost directly above that signature, there is a column, in the English it's been translated as "manager's signature." It's the last column on the right. I would just ask you if you can identify the signature that is entered on the dates of 11 July, 13 July, 15 July, 18 July, and 24 July. To my eyes they all look like they were made by the same person, do you recognise that signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Whose signature is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Milo or Milorad Nikolic. He was the person working at the gas station together with Stevo Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to him as a handler. Can you just describe what that means, sir, for us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: When a driver goes to the gas station they start fueling his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Am I correct that this Mr. Nikolic was basically the guy at the gas station at Karakaj, at the brigade station that filled up the gas for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look to our left on this document, the way we have this in our electronic version, it looks like this is all sort of one page, but if we look on the left-hand side, is it the case that that is actually the back of the document, the last page of the document because this is folded in the middle; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at the big column in the middle, if we could scroll up just a little bit, please. Little bit more. Little bit more. Perfect. Thank you. We see that that big column is headed -- it's been translated as "condition", that refers to the condition of the vehicle and we spoke about that a little earlier, did we not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it is at this point that somebody from your unit has to sign off on the condition of the vehicle; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this log and we look at the entry for July 11th and 12th, 14th and 15th, 18th and 19th, 21st and the 24th, those signatures all look the same to my layperson's eye. Do you recognise the signatures on those entries?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may go to the next page, please. Do you see the column 20 to the far right, the user's signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see your signature there in that column?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO SAKOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I see that on the computer the legibility is pretty poor. I'm going to hand you the actual original of the log. I'd be happy to give my friends an opportunity to look at it as well, but if you could just read the dates as best as you can for the entries that bear your signature, please, into the record. Just so we can be sure, because I don't think you will be able to see the dates on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if possible, could we have the document placed on the ELMO so that we can all follow the dates and then we can keep on discussing this document. We really can't see that in the electronic version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you are going to have to look at the -- I'm sorry, the original on the ELMO there. And again, just as quickly as you can just read the dates for the entries that bear your signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
